description: EarthEcho is a solo team focused on Earth science, data analysis, and interactive storytelling. Its project, Case Closed?, turns NASA Earth data into detective cases. Players make a guess, explore trends, test how changing the time window affects the evidence, and rewrite misleading claims. The goal is to make uncertainty and fair comparisons understandable through hands-on learning. Not recruiting additional members.
summary:
Can changing a starting year change what the evidence supports? Case Closed? turns NASA Earth data into interactive detective cases for students and the public.

Across 12 guided cases and eight cities, players make a guess, watch annual data unfold, and investigate the direction, size and uncertainty of environmental trends. The tool combines satellite and model data with Mann-Kendall tests, Sen's slopes, confidence intervals, and corrections for autocorrelation and multiple testing.

Its central experiment lets players move the starting year and see how the evidence changes. In Cairo, shifting the start from 2007 to 2008 changes the trend verdict, without changing any observations. Players then evaluate a misleading claim, adopt a more accurate statement, and export a case report.

NASA Giovanni and AppEEARS supply data on temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, sunlight, aerosols and vegetation. Cross-checks expose disagreements between sources instead of hiding them. Available in English and Chinese, Case Closed? helps people understand that a fair environmental claim must name its years, sources and limitations.
details:
View the 7-slide presentation: https://github.com/Maple-0102/case-closed/blob/main/docs/case-closed-slides.pdf

WHAT IT DOES

Case Closed? is an interactive Earth-science investigation for students and the public. It helps users examine what is changing, where, by how much, and how strong the evidence is.

Users enter through the home-page case wall, 12 guided case cards, an interactive world map, or a case builder that suggests combinations from the available locations and variables. The current version covers eight cities and seven measures, including model and satellite precipitation.

THE INVESTIGATION

1. Choose a case and make a prediction.

2. Watch annual data unfold on an animated chart.

3. Read the trend direction, magnitude, uncertainty and evidence verdict.

4. Compare other places, related variables and available alternative data sources.

5. Move the starting year to test how sensitive the conclusion is to the chosen time window.

6. Evaluate a claim, read the explanation, and adopt a corrected statement.

7. Export a case report containing the evidence, sources, conclusion and remaining questions.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

The central interaction makes cherry-picking something users can experience. In Cairo, the 2001–2025 haze record does not pass the project's trend criterion, while the checked windows starting in 2008–2011 and ending in 2025 do. Moving the start from 2007 to 2008 changes the verdict without changing the underlying observations.

This does not identify when the decline began. It demonstrates why a claim must retain the years it describes. The final claim-checking activity turns that lesson into a practical skill: explaining what the evidence supports without overstating it.

DATA AND METHODS

NASA Giovanni provides monthly regional averages from MERRA-2, MODIS Terra and Aqua, and GPM IMERG. AppEEARS provides MODIS vegetation data and quality information. NASA GISTEMP supplies global temperature context, and NASA POWER provides an additional model-data comparison. NOAA weather stations provide a separate temperature cross-check.

The analysis uses Mann-Kendall trend tests, Sen's slopes, 95% slope intervals, a lag-1 autocorrelation adjustment, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across locations. Missing observations are not invented. Coverage limitations and differences between model and satellite measurements are explained.

Validation against pymannkendall and SciPy covered three cities' temperature series. Uncorrected Mann-Kendall statistics and Sen's slopes matched the reference implementations; confidence-interval endpoints differed slightly because of interpolation conventions. This is a bounded implementation check, not validation of every dataset or correction.

UNCERTAINTY AND LIMITATIONS

"Not proven" does not mean "no change." A trend does not establish its cause. Variables from the same model are not treated as independent confirmation. Where sources disagree, the disagreement is shown as an open question.

The current map and case builder use predefined locations and datasets. Arbitrary-location analysis and expanded classroom lessons are future work. The intended benefit is improved understanding of environmental evidence; learning outcomes have not yet been formally evaluated.

IMPLEMENTATION

The application uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript and SVG, with Python for data preparation and Node.js for tests. It runs as a static website on GitHub Pages, supports English and Chinese, and requires no installation. Source data, processing scripts and method documentation are available in the public repository.

AI ASSISTANCE

Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex assisted with code, debugging, writing, review and demo-video editing. The demo includes AI-generated narration, as disclosed in its description. Environmental observations come from the cited datasets, not from generative AI.
